summary: Egypt issues a 30-day tourist eVisa through its official portal visa2egypt.gov.eg (30 USD single entry, 65 USD multiple entry) and sells the same visa on arrival for 30 USD cash to a broad list of nationalities, including the US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia and Japan; visitors flying directly to the Sinai Red Sea resorts can instead use a free 15-day Sinai-only entry stamp.

notes: Drones are banned in Egypt without a hard-to-get military permit — do not bring one, even packed away; they are confiscated and travelers have been detained.
Exporting antiquities or anything that looks like one is a serious criminal offense. Buy souvenirs from licensed shops and keep receipts.
Satellite phones and some radio equipment require prior authorization.

payments.text: Cards work in hotels, resort restaurants and larger shops, but Egypt runs on cash: bazaars, taxis, site entrance extras and tips (baksheesh) all need small notes. ATMs are common in cities and resorts. Carry small-denomination pounds.

safety.text: Main tourist areas (Cairo, Luxor, Aswan, the Nile Valley and Red Sea resorts) are heavily policed and generally safe for visitors, but avoid the North Sinai governorate and the Western Desert near the Libyan border, and expect security checkpoints when traveling between cities.

bestTimeToVisit.text: October to April brings mild, sunny weather ideal for the pyramids and Nile Valley sites; summer is extremely hot inland, though Red Sea resorts stay busy year-round.

tips.text: Apply for the Egyptian eVisa only at the official portal visa2egypt.gov.eg — look-alike sites charge large markups on the 30 USD fee and sometimes deliver nothing.
Drones are illegal to bring into Egypt without a military permit, even packed in luggage. They are confiscated at the airport and can lead to detention.

Flying directly to Sharm El Sheikh, Dahab, Nuweiba or Taba and staying in South Sinai? You can get a free 15-day Sinai-only entry stamp instead of a visa, but it does not cover Cairo, Luxor or diving trips to Ras Mohammed by boat, so most excursion-takers still buy the full visa.

Never photograph military installations, checkpoints or bridges — cameras and phones can be seized. Small tips (baksheesh) are a routine part of daily life for guides, drivers and washroom attendants; keep 5–20 EGP notes handy.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Egypt?
faq.answer: Yes. US passport holders need a 30-day tourist visa, obtainable either as an eVisa at visa2egypt.gov.eg (30 USD single entry, 65 USD multiple entry) or on arrival for 30 USD cash at the airport bank counters before immigration. Both grant the same 30-day stay.

faq.question: Is Egypt's visa on arrival better than the eVisa?
faq.answer: Both grant the same 30-day stay. The eVisa costs 30 USD, paid online by card; the paper visa on arrival costs 30 USD in cash at the airport counters before immigration, and at Cairo International Airport it is also sold as a QR code by card for 36 USD (including a 6 USD digital service fee). The eVisa avoids the airport queue and is safer if your airline checks visas before boarding. The two lists are not identical: Chinese, Indian and Vietnamese citizens, among others, can use the eVisa but not the visa on arrival, while Jordanian and Lebanese citizens can get the visa on arrival under conditions.

faq.question: What is the free Sinai entry stamp?
faq.answer: Travelers arriving directly at Sharm El Sheikh, Taba or other South Sinai airports can get a free entry stamp allowing 15 days in the South Sinai resorts (Sharm, Dahab, Nuweiba, Taba) without a visa. It does not allow travel to Cairo, Luxor or the rest of Egypt — for that you need the regular 30-day visa.

faq.question: How long must my passport be valid to enter Egypt?
faq.answer: At least 6 months from your date of arrival. Airlines enforce this at check-in, so renew your passport first if you are close to the limit.

faq.question: Do I need vaccinations for Egypt?
faq.answer: No vaccinations are required for arrivals from Europe, North America or most of Asia. A yellow fever certificate (ICVP) is required only if you arrive from or transited through a yellow fever risk country, such as much of sub-Saharan Africa or South America.
